people.name: Sami Rasouli
body: For about 18 years, people walking down Nicollet Avenue in south Minneapolis could stop at Sinbad's Cafe and Market for fresh bread, groceries from across the Middle East, and a hot meal. Behind the counter was Sami Rasouli. Community Peacemaker Teams credits him with helping introduce Arab culture to the Twin Cities.

Rasouli was born and raised in Najaf, Iraq, and worked as a schoolteacher. By the Hawkinson Foundation's account, he left Iraq at 24 to teach in the United Arab Emirates and then in Germany. He settled in Minnesota in 1986, drove a cab until he could buy the cafe and market, and became a U.S. citizen in 2001.

In 2003 he went back to Iraq for his mother's funeral, his first visit in 27 years. What he saw changed the direction of his life. In 2004 he sold the business and moved back to help rebuild. He worked with Christian Peacemaker Teams, now Community Peacemaker Teams, and in the spring of 2005 Muslim Peacemaker Teams began in Iraq with him as its founder and leader. Its work included nonviolence training, youth programs and vocational training for women.

He did not cut his ties to Minnesota. Supporters here started the Iraqi and American Reconciliation Project, incorporated as a nonprofit in 2007, which partnered with Muslim Peacemaker Teams. Letter exchanges between students and donated water filtration systems for Najaf schools and hospitals led to a sister-city resolution, which the Minneapolis City Council passed in July 2009. By 2013, eight delegations of Iraqi professionals, artists and citizens had traveled from Najaf to Minneapolis, and Rasouli had hosted many American visits to Najaf.
As of a March 2026 account from Community Peacemaker Teams, he was supporting a training in Iraq and returning to the Twin Cities once a year to speak about Iraq.
keyFacts: Born and raised in Najaf, Iraq; worked as a schoolteacher.
1986: Settled in Minnesota; ran Sinbad's Cafe and Market on Nicollet Avenue for about 18 years.
2001: Became a U.S. citizen.
2003: Returned to Iraq for his mother's funeral; 2004: sold the business and moved back.
2005: Muslim Peacemaker Teams began in Iraq.
July 2009: The Minneapolis City Council approved Najaf as a sister city.
2013: Hawkinson Foundation honorary award.
people.connectToWork: If someone's sense of home spans two countries, how would you ask what that means for their plans, travel or family duties, instead of assuming it?

people.name: Hend Al-Mansour
body: Picture a gallery wall covered with bright silkscreen prints of Arab and Muslim women, drawn with bold lines and patterns, sometimes framed by Arabic calligraphy. The artist who made them, Hend Al-Mansour, started her career with a stethoscope.

Al-Mansour was born in 1956 in Hofuf, in eastern Saudi Arabia. She earned her medical degree at Cairo University in 1981 and practiced medicine in Saudi Arabia for nearly two decades, training in cardiology in Riyadh. In 1997 a cardiology fellowship at the Mayo Clinic in Rochester brought her to Minnesota, and she soon found herself more drawn to art. She earned a Master of Fine Arts from the Minneapolis College of Art and Design in 2002 and a master's in art history from the University of St. Thomas in 2013.

Her screen prints, installations and portraits address women's rights, bodies and gender inequality, often drawing on images of Arab and Muslim women. MPR News profiled her in 2014, when she was working at Highpoint Center for Printmaking in Minneapolis and living in St. Paul. She received a McKnight Visual Artist Fellowship in 2018, and her resume lists a 2025 exhibition at the Minneapolis Institute of Art, Mihrab: Portraits of Arab American Women.
keyFacts: 1956: Born in Hofuf, Saudi Arabia.
1981: Medical degree (MB, BCh), Cairo University.
1997: Moved to Minnesota for a cardiology fellowship at the Mayo Clinic.
2002: MFA, Minneapolis College of Art and Design.
2013: M.A. in art history, University of St. Thomas.
2018: McKnight Visual Artist Fellowship.
2025: Mihrab: Portraits of Arab American Women, Minneapolis Institute of Art.
people.connectToWork: What training, licenses or careers from another country does your process leave out when it asks about a person's work history?

people.name: Lana Barkawi
body: Each year in the Twin Cities, the lights go down in a theater and an audience settles in to watch films from across the Arab world and its diaspora. Before the first film starts, Lana Barkawi steps up to open the Twin Cities Arab Film Festival.

As of October 2026, Barkawi is the executive and artistic director of Mizna, the St. Paul arts organization profiled on this page. She publishes its journal, Mizna: SWANA Literature and Art, and produces the festival. SWANA stands for Southwest Asia and North Africa. Mizna's staff page notes that she holds a doctorate in biochemistry and links that training to her collaborative, discovery-based way of working. She has also served on grant panels for funders including the Knight Foundation and the National Endowment for the Arts.

In 2019 Mizna marked 20 years of publishing, and public radio covered the anniversary. "I say every year when I open the film festival, it feels like our work is more important now than ever," Barkawi said. In April 2023 Mizna named Ellina Kevorkian deputy director to work alongside her, a hire tied to growth supported by a multi-year McKnight Foundation award.

Publisher of Mizna: SWANA Literature and Art; producer of the Twin Cities Arab Film Festival.

people.name: Nabil Matar
body: Most Americans learn the history of the 1500s and 1600s as a story of Europeans sailing outward. Nabil Matar has spent his career reading the other side of the record: letters, travel accounts and documents showing that people from North Africa and the Ottoman world were also traveling, trading, negotiating and writing about Europe.

Matar earned his bachelor's and master's degrees at the American University of Beirut and a Ph.D. in English at Cambridge University in 1976. He taught at the University of Jordan and the American University of Beirut. In 1986 he moved to the United States to teach at the Florida Institute of Technology, where he headed the humanities department from 1997 to 2007.

In 2007 he joined the University of Minnesota, where he became a Presidential Professor and, in 2017, Samuel Russell Chair in the Humanities. The university's profile lists him as teaching in the English and History departments and the Religious Studies Program.

His books include Islam in Britain, 1558–1685 (1998), Turks, Moors and Englishmen in the Age of Discovery (1999) and Britain and Barbary, 1589–1689 (2005). Others, such as In the Lands of the Christians (2003) and Europe through Arab Eyes, 1578–1727 (2009), bring Arabic writings about Europe to English readers. In 2018 he gave the Farhat J. Ziadeh Distinguished Lecture at the University of Washington.
keyFacts: B.A. and M.A., American University of Beirut.
1976: Ph.D., Cambridge University.
1986: Moved to the U.S. to teach at the Florida Institute of Technology.
1998, 1999, 2005: Published three books on Britain and the Islamic world.
2007: Joined the University of Minnesota.
2017: Named Samuel Russell Chair in the Humanities.
people.connectToWork: When a training or document you use frames two regions as opposites, whose records would you read to check that picture?

people.name: Ahmed Tharwat
body: On community television in the Twin Cities, viewers have been able to tune in to BelAhdan, an Arab American talk show. The Arabic name is usually translated as "With Open Arms." Its host and producer is Ahmed Tharwat, who grew up in Egypt and lives in Minnesota.

Days after September 11, 2001, he wrote a Star Tribune commentary on the dilemma his community faced that week and appeared on Twin Cities Public Television's Almanac, on a segment titled Arab American Fear. The program identified him as an Arab, a Muslim and a Minnesotan.

He has also reached listeners and readers through other outlets. As an MPR News commentator in 2010, he told a story about how much feta cheese means to an Egyptian immigrant. In 2015 he wrote a column series, Notes from America, for Daily News Egypt, explaining American life to Egyptian readers. Work like this runs in two directions: Arab life for Minnesotans, and Minnesota for readers abroad.
keyFacts: Grew up in Egypt; lives in Minnesota.
Host and producer of BelAhdan, an Arab American television show.
September 2001: Star Tribune commentary and TPT Almanac appearance.
2010: MPR News essay on feta cheese and Egyptian immigrant life.
2015: Notes from America columns for Daily News Egypt.
people.connectToWork: When events abroad or in the news may be weighing on someone, how would you make room for that without assuming how they feel about it?

people.name: Edward Said
body: In 1999, young musicians from Israel and several Arab countries met in Weimar, Germany, to rehearse together. Many had never met someone from the other side. The workshop became the West-Eastern Divan Orchestra. Its founders were the conductor Daniel Barenboim and a Columbia University literature professor named Edward Said.

Said was born in Jerusalem in 1935 into a Palestinian Christian family. His father, Wadie, had volunteered for the U.S. Army in World War I, which made Said an American citizen. He grew up between Jerusalem and Cairo and later came to the United States for school. The displacement of Palestinians after 1948, which Palestinians call the Nakba, or "catastrophe," shaped his family and his thinking.

In 1963 he began teaching at Columbia University, where he became University Professor of English and Comparative Literature. In 1978 he published Orientalism. The book argued that Western scholarship, literature and art often portrayed "the East," including the Arab world, as exotic, backward or dangerous, and that these images supported colonial power. It became a founding text of postcolonial studies and has also drawn debate.
Said was a public voice for Palestinian rights in the United States, and a pianist and music critic. He lived with leukemia for about a decade and died in New York in September 2003, at 67.
keyFacts: 1935: Born in Jerusalem; a U.S. citizen through his father's World War I service in the U.S. Army.
1963: Began teaching at Columbia University.
1978: Published Orientalism.
1999: Began the West-Eastern Divan Orchestra with Daniel Barenboim.
September 2003: Died in New York, after about a decade with leukemia.
people.connectToWork: Look at the images and stories your team uses about people from another region. Who made them, and what would you ask before using them again?

people.name: Naomi Shihab Nye
body: In 1966, a 14-year-old girl from St. Louis moved with her family to the West Bank, then part of Jordan. For about a year she lived among her Palestinian relatives and saw the land her family came from. That year became a lifelong source for her poems.

Naomi Shihab Nye was born on March 12, 1952, in St. Louis, Missouri. Her father, Aziz Shihab, was a Palestinian journalist who became a refugee in 1948. Her mother was American. Before the 1967 war the family left the West Bank and settled in San Antonio, Texas.

Nye is the author or editor of more than 30 volumes, including poetry, essays, novels and picture books. She describes herself as a "wandering poet" who leads writing workshops. Her poems often turn on small daily details, such as a grandmother's hands or a kind act between strangers, and she has edited collections that bring poets from many regions to young American readers.
She received the 2013 Neustadt Award for Children's Literature. In 2019 the Poetry Foundation named her Young People's Poet Laureate for the 2019–2021 term.
keyFacts: March 12, 1952: Born in St. Louis, Missouri, to a Palestinian father and an American mother.
1966: Moved with her family to the West Bank; settled in San Antonio before the 1967 war.
Author or editor of more than 30 volumes.
2013: Neustadt Award for Children's Literature.
2019: Named Young People's Poet Laureate (2019–2021 term).

people.name: Ahmed Zewail
body: A chemical reaction happens almost too fast to imagine. Bonds between atoms break and form in femtoseconds; one femtosecond is a millionth of a billionth of a second. For most of history, scientists could see only the beginning and end of a reaction. Ahmed Zewail found a way to watch the middle.

Zewail was born on February 26, 1946, in Damanhur, Egypt. He earned degrees at Alexandria University in 1967 and 1969 and a doctorate from the University of Pennsylvania in 1974. In 1976 he joined the faculty of the California Institute of Technology (Caltech), where he later held the Linus Pauling professorship. He became a U.S. citizen in 1982.

At Caltech, Zewail and his team used extremely fast laser pulses, like a high-speed camera, to take snapshots of molecules as they reacted. The field became known as femtochemistry, and in 1999 he alone received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for it. His obituary describes him as the first Egyptian to win a Nobel in science.

He stayed connected to both countries. After Egypt's 2011 revolution he became the first chair of the board of trustees of Zewail City of Science and Technology, and he received Egypt's highest state honor. He died on August 2, 2016, at age 70.
keyFacts: February 26, 1946: Born in Damanhur, Egypt.
1974: Ph.D., University of Pennsylvania.
1976: Joined the faculty of Caltech.
1982: Became a U.S. citizen.
1999: Nobel Prize in Chemistry for femtochemistry.
August 2, 2016: Died at age 70.
people.connectToWork: When someone came here as a student or scientist, how does your process learn about that history before making assumptions about what they need?

people.name: Farouk El-Baz
body: When Apollo astronauts landed on the Moon between 1969 and 1972, someone had to help decide where: safe enough to land on and scientifically worth the trip. One of those people was a young Egyptian geologist, Farouk El-Baz.

El-Baz was born in January 1938 in Zagazig, in Egypt's Nile Delta. He earned a bachelor's degree at Ain Shams University in Cairo in 1958 and then a master's and doctorate in geology in the United States. In 1967 he joined Bellcomm, which gave engineering support to NASA headquarters, and studied the photographs sent back by NASA's Lunar Orbiter spacecraft. He became secretary of the Apollo Landing Site Selection Committee and chaired the astronaut training group of the Apollo photo team, helping astronauts describe lunar geology from orbit.

After Apollo, he turned to deserts. He used satellite images to study desert landforms and helped show how remote sensing could help locate groundwater. In 1986 he became director of the Center for Remote Sensing at Boston University, and he led it until he retired in spring 2018. That year Case Western Reserve University awarded him the Inamori Ethics Prize, citing his Apollo work and his search for groundwater in dry regions such as Darfur.
keyFacts: January 1938: Born in Zagazig, Egypt.
1967: Joined Bellcomm; secretary of the Apollo Landing Site Selection Committee.
1969–1972: Apollo crews landed at sites his committee helped select.
1986–2018: Director, Center for Remote Sensing, Boston University.
2018: Inamori Ethics Prize.
people.connectToWork: What knowledge of a place or a home country might a participant or colleague bring that your work never asks for?

people.name: Mona Hanna-Attisha
body: In 2015, a pediatrician in Flint, Michigan, went through children's health records and noticed something alarming. After the city switched its water source to the Flint River, the share of children with high levels of lead in their blood had gone up. Lead can permanently harm children's brains. When she announced her findings, the state pushed back and called her an unfortunate researcher who was causing near-hysteria. Dr. Mona Hanna-Attisha stood by her data, and the data held.

Hanna-Attisha, who now goes by Mona Hanna, was born in England in 1976. Her parents were Iraqi scientists who had left Iraq during Saddam Hussein's rise to power. The family moved to Michigan when her father took a job as an engineer with General Motors, and her mother taught English to recent immigrants.

Her research and her willingness to speak out made the Flint water crisis national news. Afterward she stayed. She leads the Pediatric Public Health Initiative, a partnership of Michigan State University and Hurley Children's Hospital, and its work includes the Rx Kids program. In 2018 she published What the Eyes Don't See, about the crisis and how Flint responded, and she has connected her drive for justice to her family's history of resistance in Iraq.
keyFacts: 1976: Born in England to Iraqi scientist parents.
2015: Her research showed rising blood lead levels in Flint children after the water source change.
State officials at first rejected her findings.
2018: Published What the Eyes Don't See.
Leads the Michigan State University and Hurley Children's Hospital Pediatric Public Health Initiative.
people.connectToWork: If your own data pointed to harm from a decision your agency made, who would you tell first, and what would help you keep going if they pushed back?

people.name: Simon Shaheen
body: Simon Shaheen was born in 1955 in Tarshiha, a largely Christian community in northern Israel, in the Galilee. He would bring the classical Arabic tradition to concert halls across the United States, playing the oud, the fretless lute at the heart of Arabic music, and the violin.

He graduated from the Academy of Music in Jerusalem in 1978, and he took part in Arabic music performances for Israeli national radio and television from 1973 to 1978. He earned a bachelor's degree in music and Arabic literature at Tel Aviv University. In 1980 he moved to New York to study at the Manhattan School of Music and Columbia University, and he earned master's degrees at both.

In New York he did more than perform. In 1982 he founded the Near Eastern Music Ensemble. He later formed Qantara, a name meaning "arch" in Arabic, a band that blends Arab, jazz, Western classical and Latin American music. His recordings include The Music of Mohamed Abdel Wahab, Taqasim, Saltanah, Blue Flame (2001) and Turath, which the Library of Congress named an outstanding traditional recording of 1992.

In 1994 the National Endowment for the Arts named him a National Heritage Fellow. In 1997 he founded the Arabic Music Retreat, a week-long summer program of intensive study at Mount Holyoke College in Massachusetts.

1978: Graduated from the Academy of Music in Jerusalem.
1980: Moved to New York.
1982: Founded the Near Eastern Music Ensemble.

people.name: Diana Abu-Jaber
body: In Diana Abu-Jaber's books, food is a language: a pot of coffee, a tray of baklava, a family argument across a crowded table. Born in Syracuse, New York, to an American mother and a Jordanian father, she has spent her career writing about family, culture and food.

Her first novel, Arabian Jazz (1993), follows a Jordanian American family in upstate New York and won the Oregon Book Award. Her second, Crescent (2003), is a love story set among Arab students and exiles in Los Angeles. It won the PEN Center USA Award for Literary Fiction and an American Book Award.

The Language of Baklava (2005) is a memoir with recipes. Her later books include the novel Origin (2007); Birds of Paradise, which won the 2012 Arab American Book Award; the culinary memoir Life Without a Recipe; the young-adult fantasy Silverworld; and the novel Fencing with the King (2022). The National Endowment for the Arts counted eight books in 2024.
She is also a teacher. Since 1996 she has been on the Portland State University faculty, where she is a professor of English.
keyFacts: Born in Syracuse, New York; Jordanian father, American mother.
1993: Arabian Jazz; Oregon Book Award.
2003: Crescent; PEN Center USA Award and American Book Award.

2012: Arab American Book Award for Birds of Paradise.
2022: Fencing with the King.
Professor of English at Portland State University, on the faculty since 1996.

people.name: Rami Malek
body: In 2019 Rami Malek walked onstage at the 91st Academy Awards to accept the Oscar for Best Actor for playing Freddie Mercury in Bohemian Rhapsody. "I am the son of immigrants from Egypt. I am a first-generation American," he told the audience. The National reported him as the first Egyptian to win that award.

Malek was born on May 12, 1981, in Los Angeles to Coptic Egyptian immigrant parents, who moved there in 1978. His father, who worked as a tour guide in Egypt and later sold insurance here, would wake him at night to speak with Arabic-speaking relatives in the family's hometown of Samalut. He spoke Egyptian Arabic at home until about age four. He graduated from the University of Evansville's theatre department in Indiana in 2003.

His early parts included a 2004 guest role on Gilmore Girls, a recurring role on The War at Home from 2005, the Night at the Museum films and HBO's The Pacific (2010). He broke out in 2015 as the hacker Elliot Alderson in Mr. Robot, which won him the 2016 Emmy. He went on to No Time to Die (2021) and Oppenheimer (2023).
keyFacts: May 12, 1981: Born in Los Angeles to Coptic Egyptian immigrant parents.
2003: Graduated from the University of Evansville (theatre).
2015: Began starring in Mr. Robot; 2016 Emmy.
2019: Academy Award for Best Actor, Bohemian Rhapsody.
2021: No Time to Die; 2023: Oppenheimer.

people.name: Dina Powell McCormick
body: Dina Habib was born in Cairo in 1973. Arabic was the only language she knew before the age of four. In 1977 her parents brought the family to Dallas, Texas, where her father, a former Egyptian Army captain, drove a bus and ran a convenience store. Four decades later she was in the White House as Deputy National Security Advisor. She now uses the name Dina Powell McCormick.

She graduated from Ursuline Academy in Dallas and from the University of Texas at Austin. She worked on the staff of House Majority Leader Dick Armey and served as Director of Congressional Affairs at the Republican National Committee.

Under President George W. Bush she became Assistant to the President for Presidential Personnel in 2003. Confirmed in June 2005, she became Assistant Secretary of State for Educational and Cultural Affairs, the office that runs international exchange programs, and principal deputy to Karen Hughes. She spent 16 years at Goldman Sachs in all, as a partner and member of its Management Committee, and she launched programs there including 10,000 Women. At the start of President Trump's first term she served as Deputy National Security Advisor.

She later became vice chair and president of BDT & MSD Partners and joined the ExxonMobil board. After a short time on Meta's board in 2025, she was named Meta's president and vice chairman in January 2026, the role the George W. Bush Presidential Center lists for her.
keyFacts: 1973: Born in Cairo; 1977: family immigrated and settled in Dallas.
2003: Assistant to the President for Presidential Personnel.
2005: Assistant Secretary of State for Educational and Cultural Affairs.
16 years at Goldman Sachs, including as partner and Management Committee member.
2017: Deputy National Security Advisor.
January 2026: Named president and vice chairman of Meta.

people.name: Mohamed A. El-Erian
body: Mohamed El-Erian was born in New York in 1958 while his father, an Egyptian diplomat, was posted there. The family returned to Cairo and moved back to New York in 1968, when his father took a United Nations job. He became one of the best-known voices on the global economy.

He studied at Cambridge and earned a master's and doctorate at Oxford. He spent about 15 years at the International Monetary Fund and worked as a managing director at Salomon Smith Barney/Citigroup. He was president and CEO of Harvard Management Company, which manages Harvard University's endowment, and later CEO and co-chief investment officer of the investment firm PIMCO, which he left in 2014.

He has written two New York Times best-sellers, including The Only Game in Town. He was President of Queens' College, Cambridge, the college where he studied, from 2020 to September 2025; Dame Menna Rawlings succeeded him on October 1, 2025. His biographies list him as chief economic adviser at Allianz and a professor of practice at the Wharton School.

Doctorate, Oxford University.
About 15 years at the International Monetary Fund.
CEO and co-chief investment officer of PIMCO; left in 2014.

people.name: Maysoon Zayid
body: In January 2014 TED posted a talk with a title that gets a laugh on its own: "I got 99 problems ... palsy is just one." The speaker was Maysoon Zayid, a Palestinian American comedian from New Jersey who has cerebral palsy.

Zayid studied theater at Arizona State University. Early in her acting career she found she would get more work by doing stand-up, and TED quotes her telling the BBC that "a fluffy ethnic disabled chick was never going to get a job unless she did stand-up." In 2003 she and comedian Dean Obeidallah co-founded the New York Arab-American Comedy Festival.

She appeared in You Don't Mess with the Zohan and has a recurring role as the lawyer Zahra Amir on General Hospital, after two years early in her career on As the World Turns. Her first graphic novel, Shiny Misfits, published by Scholastic in 2024, centers on a disabled elementary school student.

By TED's account, she spends several months a year in the Palestinian territories running art workshops for disabled and orphaned children in refugee camps. New Jersey Monthly reported in 2020 that she lives in Cliffside Park.
keyFacts: Palestinian American, from New Jersey. Studied theater at Arizona State University.
2003: Co-founded the New York Arab-American Comedy Festival with Dean Obeidallah.
2014: TED talk, "I got 99 problems ... palsy is just one."
Recurring role on General Hospital as Zahra Amir.
2024: Graphic novel Shiny Misfits (Scholastic).
Runs art workshops for disabled and orphaned children in Palestinian refugee camps.

people.name: Marina Salman
body: In November 2021 a discussion was held online that its hosts called the first of its kind: what language and framework should Arab communities use about disability? The University of Illinois Chicago's Arab American Cultural Center and Disability Cultural Center organized it, and one of the facilitators was Marina Salman.

Salman describes herself as an Arab American woman with multiple disabilities who wants to empower Arabs with disabilities to live meaningful lives. At Access Living, Chicago's center for independent living, she has worked with SOAR (SSI/SSDI Outreach, Access, and Recovery) and in community reintegration, helping people move out of nursing facilities. UIC and Disability Lead describe her as a SOAR case manager; The Triangle, Inc. called her director of SOAR in 2023.

She holds a master's degree in counseling psychology from Adler University in Chicago and was a 2023 Disability Lead fellow. Her advocacy focuses on where race and disability meet, including health care and criminal justice reform.
keyFacts: Arab American woman with multiple disabilities, in her own description.
Works with SOAR at Access Living, Chicago.
Master's in counseling psychology, Adler University.
November 16, 2021: Co-facilitated "Unlearn to Relearn: Shifting Attitudes for Arabs with Disabilities."
2023: Disability Lead fellow.

institutions.name: Mizna
institutions.type: Literary and arts organization; publisher; film festival presenter
institutions.location: St. Paul, Minnesota, 2446 University Avenue West, Suite 115
body: In 1999 Kathryn Haddad and Saleh Abudayyeh, with a small group of Arab, SWANA and Muslim writers, artists and scholars, started a grassroots literary journal so that Arab American writers would have a place to publish on their own terms. They named it Mizna. Haddad was its first executive director, from 1999 to 2009.

Public radio has described it as the nation's first Arab American literary journal, and reported that it began as an arts section in a newsletter put out by an Arab American advocacy group. It grew into an organization with a twice-yearly print journal, the digital platform Mizna Online, readings, film series, performances, public art and workshops.

In 2003 it launched the Twin Cities Arab Film Festival, which Mizna describes as the largest and longest-running SWANA-centered film festival in the Midwest. SWANA stands for Southwest Asia and North Africa. As of October 2026 the journal's current issue is 26.2, Translational, and Mizna has a film screening set for November 2, 2026, at The Main Cinema in Minneapolis (Palestine Cinema Days, Return to Haifa, 7 p.m.), and the 20th Twin Cities Arab Film Festival ran September 23 to 27, 2026. Check its calendar before planning a visit.
keyFacts: 1999: Founded by Kathryn Haddad and Saleh Abudayyeh with a small group of writers, artists and scholars.
Publishes the twice-yearly journal Mizna and Mizna Online.
2003: Launched the Twin Cities Arab Film Festival.
Based in St. Paul.
institutions.connectToWork: Where could you go to hear people speak for themselves before you plan something for them, and how would you go as a guest and not as a recruiter?

institutions.name: Arab American National Museum
body: In May 2005 the Arab American National Museum opened on Michigan Avenue in Dearborn. The museum describes itself as the first and only museum of its kind in the United States devoted to recording the Arab American experience, from the first immigrants in the late 19th century to today. It is a national institution of ACCESS and a Smithsonian Affiliate.

Its permanent exhibits have included "Coming to America," "Living in America," "Making an Impact" and "Arab Civilization: Our Heritage." In 2006 the museum established the Arab American Book Award with librarians from the University of Toledo, and the award has continued through its 2026 winners.
keyFacts: May 2005: Opened in Dearborn, Michigan.
Smithsonian Affiliate; a national institution of ACCESS.
2006: Established the Arab American Book Award.
institutions.connectToWork: How much of the history of people you serve did you learn only from others' accounts, and where could you read their own?

institutions.name: Arab American Institute
body: In 1985 James Zogby co-founded the Arab American Institute to give Arab Americans a stronger voice in American political life. As of October 2026, its staff page lists Zogby as president and Maya Berry as executive director. It polled Arab American voters ahead of the 2026 midterm election. Its foundation describes itself as a national civil rights organization that works to "strengthen democracy, protect civil rights and liberties, and defend human rights."

It is also a source of data on Arab Americans. By its own account the Census Bureau has recognized it as its only Census Information Center dedicated to analyzing data on the Arab American community, and it has been a partner in that program since 2001.

The Institute estimates there are about 3.7 million Arab Americans, while the 2020 Census counted 2,815,469. It attributes the gap to the census having no Arab or Middle Eastern and North African category, sampling limits, intermarriage over generations, and some recent immigrants' wariness of government surveys. Its demographics page lists Minnesota among the top 12 states and Minneapolis among the top six metro areas, though the same page names Virginia twice in its list of twelve states. The estimate comes from an advocacy organization, and the page gives no margin for it.
keyFacts: 1985: Co-founded by James Zogby.
Since 2001: Census Information Center partner, by its own account.
Estimates about 3.7 million Arab Americans; the 2020 Census counted 2,815,469.
institutions.connectToWork: If your data has no category for Arab or Middle Eastern and North African people, who is missing from your reports, and how would you find out?

institutions.name: ACCESS (Arab Community Center for Economic and Social Services)
aliases: Arab Community Center for Economic and Social Services
body: In 1971 volunteers opened a storefront in the south end of Dearborn, Michigan, to help Arab immigrants adjust to life in the United States. That storefront grew into ACCESS, which by its own count now has 11 locations and more than 120 programs in metro Detroit. It also runs national institutions, including the Arab American National Museum and the National Network for Arab American Communities.

Its programs include a Living with Alzheimer's Program in English and Arabic and a Recovery Center that held its ribbon cutting in September 2026. We did not find a program specifically for disability. It is not in Minnesota, and it appears here as one example of how an Arab American-led agency organizes bilingual services.
keyFacts: 1971: Founded in Dearborn, Michigan.
11 locations and more than 120 programs in metro Detroit.
Home of the Arab American National Museum and the National Network for Arab American Communities.

disability.intro: This is background for preparing questions. It does not describe any person or family. Here, Arabic-speaking covers people of many faiths and none, from many countries, and both long-settled families and recent arrivals. We did not find a Minnesota study of disability among Arabic-speaking people. The U.S. studies we could read are small, focus on parents of autistic children, and mostly include Muslim families. We found little on Christian, Druze, Iraqi refugee or Sudanese experience, or on disabilities other than autism.
questions: What words do you and your family use to describe this, in Arabic and in English? Which words would you like me to use?
Has anyone given you a diagnosis or a label? Who gave it, do you agree with it, and has it helped?
What do you want a label or assessment to open up for you? Is there anything you want it to avoid?
Who in your family helps with care, and who would you like included in decisions or meetings?
What do you believe helps most? Are there religious or family practices that matter to you and that I should know about?
Are you worried about what others might hear? Would it help if I explained who will see this information?
Which language and dialect do you prefer? Would you like a male or female interpreter, or someone from outside your local community?
What would a good life look like for you in five years?
Do you have any worries about how using a service could affect your immigration status or benefits? Would you like a referral for legal advice?

context.heading: What small U.S. studies report
body: Habayeb and colleagues (2020, Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders) surveyed 20 Arab American caregivers of children with autism and interviewed nine of them. Perceived stigma averaged low to moderate. Interviews still described the effects of disability stigma and of distancing from their communities, and parent gender roles came up as a theme. That sample does not describe any family.

A University of South Florida study by Haifa Alsayyari (2018) interviewed five Arab American mothers of children with autism. Its themes were the path to accepting the diagnosis, beliefs about causes, concerns, needs, coping, and "unanticipated positive effects."

April DeMasters (2023, Walden University dissertation) interviewed first- and second-generation Muslim Arab American immigrant parents whose children were diagnosed within the prior 15 years. Parents described difficulty telling family and community about the diagnosis, and having to work out how to get help.

context.heading: Faith and explanations, from outside the U.S.
body: A disability-awareness resource from New Zealand's eCALD program describes explanations found in some families, drawing on research that includes Kuwaiti mothers and Pakistani families. It is not U.S. evidence. It mentions disability as divine intervention with a reason and the evil eye, and notes that the evil eye appears among Middle Eastern Christians as well, and that some devout Muslims reject talismans as superstition. It stresses that religious and medical explanations can sit together, that family members can disagree, and that religious belief often helps families cope.

If someone raises faith, ask whether a faith leader or practice is important to them and whether they want it included. Ask what produced an impairment only as a question the person may choose to answer.

sources.label: eCALD (New Zealand), "Beliefs about causes of disability"

context.heading: Words, dialects and interpreters
body: We found no source documenting specific Arabic words for disability or which ones carry stigma, so none are offered here. A November 2021 discussion held by the University of Illinois Chicago's Arab American and Disability Cultural Centers asked this very question: what language and framework should Arab communities use?

Ask the person which words they use. Ask interpreters how a term will be rendered, and avoid words that mean "sick" or "crazy" when the meaning is disabled. Spoken Arabic differs by region, so ask about the dialect when you request an interpreter. Use trained professional interpreters, not children or relatives, and check understanding by having the person explain it back in their own words.

sources.label: University of Illinois Chicago, "Unlearn to Relearn: Shifting Attitudes for Arabs with Disabilities" (2021)

context.heading: Disabled Arab American leadership and what we could not find
body: Marina Salman and Maysoon Zayid, profiled on this page, are two disabled Arab American people working in public. Salman co-facilitated the 2021 discussion in Chicago, and Zayid has written and performed openly about cerebral palsy. Neither speaks for everyone.

We did not find a Minnesota organization focused on disability among Arabic-speaking families. The one Minnesota disability figure for any Arab group is from Minnesota Compass, which reports that 13.0 percent of Lebanese Minnesotans have a disability (give or take 4.3 points); this older, mostly U.S.-born group does not represent recent arrivals. We also found no source documenting immigration or public-benefit fears for this group in disability services, so ask and refer for legal advice instead of assuming. Check shifts, transport, cost and agency rules before reading a missed appointment as cultural.

sources.label: University of Illinois Chicago, "Unlearn to Relearn" (2021)
TED, Maysoon Zayid speaker page

organizations.intro: Arabic-speaking Minnesotans include long-established Lebanese and Syrian Christian families and newer arrivals from Iraq, Palestine, Egypt, Yemen, Sudan and elsewhere. In the institutions we could confirm, people organize through churches, mosques, civil rights groups, student groups and the arts. We did not find a Minnesota-based Arabic-language news outlet, or Iraqi, Sudanese, Yemeni or Palestinian associations with a public record we could open. The list is not complete. These are starting points for learning, and listing here says nothing about who a person trusts.
